articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Designates International Criminal Court, and Removes Burma-Related Designation
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics. Concurrently, OFAC designated the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued related General Licenses.

In a separate action, OFAC also announced the removal of a Burma-related designation. These actions reflect OFAC's ongoing efforts to enforce sanctions programs and adapt to evolving geopolitical landscapes.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations, Issues General License, and Amends Russia-Related General License

In a separate but related action, OFAC also issued an amended Russia-related General License. These measures underscore the U.S. government's continued focus on both Iran and Russia in its sanctions policy.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes and Updates Designations, Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ

Additionally, OFAC published an Iran-related Alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). The alert warns foreign financial institutions that continue to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions that they could be targeted at any time without advance notification. The amended FAQ removes language suggesting OFAC would generally contact foreign financial institutions before finding them engaged in sanctionable activity.

articles.headline: Global Markets Show Mixed Trading Amid Inflation Concerns and Geopolitical Tensions
body: Global equity markets are experiencing mixed trading as investors weigh strong earnings prospects against persistent inflation concerns and geopolitical developments. U.S. futures for the S&P 500, Nasdaq 100, and Dow are hovering near unchanged, with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 testing record highs.

However, energy prices and bond yields remain elevated due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which is threatening further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve. Technology stocks, despite driving recent market gains, are showing volatility, with companies like Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices experiencing declines.

The dollar index is holding above 102 as markets await key inflation reports this week, including the September consumer and producer price indexes. A stronger-than-expected inflation reading could intensify pressure on the Fed for a more aggressive tightening path, though markets currently price an 83% chance of no rate hike this month, with an 86% probability of a December hike.

articles.headline: U.S. Inflation Expected to Remain Elevated as CPI and PPI Data Loom
body: U.S. inflation is expected to remain stubbornly high, with economists anticipating that the September Consumer Price Index (CPI), due Wednesday, will show an increase to 3.6% from 3.4% in August. The Producer Price Index (PPI), to be released on Thursday, is also projected to indicate persistent inflationary pressures.

The Federal Reserve's staff estimated that total Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price inflation edged up to 3.8% in August, driven by a pickup in consumer energy prices. Core PCE inflation, excluding food and energy, was estimated at 3.4%. These figures, higher than a year earlier, are attributed to past tariff increases, elevated energy and input costs from geopolitical developments, and rising technology-related consumer goods prices due to the AI buildout.

Despite these pressures, market-implied measures of inflation compensation remain consistent with expectations that PCE inflation will return to 2% over the medium term under appropriate monetary policy. However, many participants in Federal Open Market Committee meetings have noted elevated short-term inflation expectations and increased cost pressures reported by businesses.
articles.source: AP News / Federal Reserve / Trading Economics

articles.headline: Global Central Banks Maintain Focus on Inflation Amid Resilient Growth and Geopolitical Risks
body: Central banks globally remain focused on inflation risks, with the European Central Bank (ECB) having recently raised its policy rate due to continued inflationary pressures stemming from the Middle East conflict. Investors now anticipate further tightening from the ECB, as elevated energy prices are expected to contribute to underlying inflation and rising bond yields across Europe.

In the U.S., while markets are pricing in a high probability of the Federal Reserve keeping interest rates unchanged this month, a quarter-point rate increase in December is fully priced in. Fed Governor Christopher Waller recently indicated that further rate increases would likely be necessary to achieve the 2% inflation target, but also noted flexibility in the pace of tightening.

Other central banks are also navigating inflationary environments; DBS expects the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to keep the door open for another rate hike in December, and Singapore's central bank is expected to announce another modest tightening this week. The Bank of Japan's officials' commentary and the Reserve Bank of Australia's meeting minutes will also be closely watched by investors.

articles.headline: Oil Prices Jump Amid Middle East Conflict, Influencing Global Inflation and Market Volatility
body: Oil prices have seen a significant jump, with Brent crude rising 2% to $106.77 per barrel, contributing to market volatility. Prices have fluctuated between $96 and nearly $110 over the past month, largely due to uncertainty surrounding the U.S. conflict with Iran and its impact on global energy supplies and inflation.

The surge in energy prices is a key factor driving elevated inflation globally. In the eurozone, consumer prices were up 3.8% in September from a year earlier, with an 18.8% increase in energy prices being a primary contributor. Similarly, in the U.S., a pickup in consumer energy prices led to an increase in total PCE price inflation in August.

Despite the overall upward trend, oil prices declined on Monday due to hopes that Russian diesel could alleviate global fuel shortages. President Trump announced that Moscow agreed to release diesel fuel to global markets and claimed an 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine would take effect immediately.
articles.source: AP News / Trading Economics / Deloitte Insights

articles.headline: EU Adopts Nearly 1,600 New Sanctions Against Russia's Military Industry
body: EU foreign ministers have approved nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia's military-industrial complex, marking the 'single largest expansion' of the EU's sanctions list since the war in Ukraine began in February 2022. More than half of these new listings are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles, aiming to make it significantly harder, slower, and more expensive for Russia to produce weapons.

In addition to the Russia-related sanctions, the EU Council has extended its sanctions framework targeting the proliferation and use of chemical weapons for five years, until October 30, 2031. The validity of individual sanctions listings under this framework has also been extended for one year, until October 30, 2027, applying to 31 individuals and six entities.
These restrictive measures include asset freezes, prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available to listed individuals and entities, and travel bans to the EU for the individuals.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express National Bank for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah. The penalty was imposed due to significant deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program.

The OCC determined that American Express National Bank failed to establish and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program reasonably designed to assure and monitor compliance with the BSA and its implementing regulations. Key deficiencies included inadequate resources, staff lacking sufficient expertise, systemic internal control gaps, weak independent testing, and insufficient BSA/AML training for employees and directors.

The bank also failed to tailor its BSA/AML risk assessment to its business activities, focusing too narrowly on demand deposit accounts while neglecting the risks in its more dominant credit and charge card products. These failures contributed to systemic breakdowns in suspicious activity monitoring and reporting, resulting in the bank's inability to timely identify and report approximately $13 billion of suspected trade-based money laundering activity over the past decade.

articles.headline: BIS Adds Over Three Dozen Entities to Entity List, Citing National Security Concerns
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has added more than three dozen companies to its Entity List, effective immediately. These entities, primarily from China (28), but also including those from Belarus, Burma, Pakistan, Russia, and Taiwan, are deemed to be involved in activities contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States.

Nearly half of the listed entities, all based in China, were found to be supporting Chinese military modernization and sanctioned parties in Iran. BIS also added a significant number of Chinese and Pakistani entities for their involvement in ballistic missile and unsafeguarded nuclear activities. Several entities in Russia, Belarus, and one in Taiwan were added for supporting Russia's military, while a half dozen entities were listed for supporting human rights violations in China and Burma through surveillance programs.

Parties on the Entity List are subject to restrictive licensing requirements and policies, and companies with cross-border dealings are advised to frequently screen their counterparties to capture these changes. This action marks the second round of restrictions imposed by the U.S. in as many weeks, underscoring a continued focus on export controls.

articles.headline: BIS Strengthens Export Controls on Advanced Computing and Semiconductor Manufacturing Items to China
body: The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued a Final Rule and an Interim Final Rule on December 2, 2024, to strengthen export controls on advanced computing items and semiconductor manufacturing items to China. The Final Rule added 140 entities to the Entity List and removed three from the Validated End-User (VEU) Program, specifically targeting advanced-node integrated circuit production and semiconductor manufacturing activities.

The Interim Final Rule introduced new foreign direct product rules and Export Control Classification Numbers (ECCNs) for advanced computing and semiconductor manufacturing items. These rules became effective on December 2, 2024, with some delayed compliance dates, and comments on the Interim Final Rule were accepted until January 31, 2025.

These amendments to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) underscore the U.S. government's commitment to preventing China from acquiring critical technologies that could be used against U.S. national security interests.

articles.headline: BIS Eases Export Controls for United Arab Emirates, Upgrading Status
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced on July 10, 2026, that it will significantly upgrade the status of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). This decision recognizes the UAE's status as a U.S. Major Defense Partner and its support in advancing U.S. national security interests, including Operation Epic Fury.

As a result of this reclassification, the UAE will be removed from EAR Country Groups D:3 and D:4. This change will eliminate restrictions on support for the UAE's unmanned aerial vehicle programs, among other things, easing export controls for the nation.
This deregulatory action reflects a strategic adjustment in U.S. export policy, aiming to strengthen partnerships with key allies while continuing to protect national security interests.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
